name: Network+ Fundamentals
description: Networking fundamentals covering subnetting, OSI model application, common protocols, and basic troubleshooting methodology.

teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
```
Given: 192.168.1.0/24, divide into 4 equal subnets

Step 1: Calculate bits needed
  - 4 subnets requires 2 bits (2^2 = 4)
  - New prefix: /24 + 2 = /26

Step 2: Calculate subnet size
  - /26 means 32-26 = 6 host bits
  - Hosts per subnet: 2^6 - 2 = 62 usable
  - Subnet size: 64 addresses (0-63, 64-127, etc.)

Step 3: List subnets
  - 192.168.1.0/26   (hosts: .1-.62, broadcast: .63)
  - 192.168.1.64/26  (hosts: .65-.126, broadcast: .127)
  - 192.168.1.128/26 (hosts: .129-.190, broadcast: .191)
  - 192.168.1.192/26 (hosts: .193-.254, broadcast: .255)
```
teachingBlocks.explanation: Subnetting divides a network into smaller segments. The key insight is that each additional bit borrowed from host bits doubles your subnet count but halves available hosts. The formula 2^n gives you subnets (n = borrowed bits), and 2^h - 2 gives usable hosts (h = remaining host bits, minus network and broadcast addresses). This is fundamental to network design and troubleshooting.

surfaceVariants.description: Subnet a Class B network for multiple departments

hints: First determine how many bits you need to borrow: 2^n >= required subnets
The subnet size is always a power of 2 (64, 128, 256)
Remember: network address is first, broadcast is last, usable hosts are in between

commonErrors.description: Counted network and broadcast as usable hosts
commonErrors.remediation: Every subnet loses 2 addresses: the network address (all host bits 0) and broadcast (all host bits 1)
The increment equals the subnet size: if /26, increment is 64 (0, 64, 128, 192)

teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
```
Troubleshooting a user who can't access a website:

Layer 1 - Physical:
  Check: Cable connected? Link light on?
  Tool: Visual inspection, cable tester

Layer 2 - Data Link:
  Check: Getting MAC address? Switch port errors?
  Tool: ip link show, switch port stats

Layer 3 - Network:
  Check: IP address assigned? Can ping gateway?
  Tool: ip addr, ping 192.168.1.1

Layer 4 - Transport:
  Check: Port 443 open? Firewall blocking?
  Tool: ss -tulnp, telnet host 443

Layer 7 - Application:
  Check: DNS resolving? HTTP response?
  Tool: host example.com, curl -I https://example.com

Diagnosis: Work bottom-up until you find the failing layer.
```
teachingBlocks.explanation: The OSI model provides a systematic troubleshooting framework. Start at Layer 1 (physical) and work up. If Layer 3 (ping) works but Layer 4 (port connection) fails, you've localized the problem. This methodology prevents random troubleshooting and ensures you don't miss obvious issues. Most real-world problems occur at Layers 1, 3, or 7.

surfaceVariants.description: Analyze a TCP connection failure at Layer 4

data.scenario: SYN sent but no SYN-ACK received
ping by IP works, ping by hostname fails

hints: Always start at Layer 1 - is it plugged in?
If ping works, Layers 1-3 are probably fine
DNS issues are Layer 7 - check with host or nslookup

commonErrors.description: Jumped to application troubleshooting without checking basics
commonErrors.remediation: Always verify physical connectivity and IP configuration before checking applications

commonErrors.description: Mixed up what happens at each layer

teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
```
Essential protocols and ports:

Remote Access:
  SSH     - TCP 22  (secure shell)
  RDP     - TCP 3389 (Windows remote desktop)
  Telnet  - TCP 23  (insecure, avoid)

Web Services:
  HTTP    - TCP 80  (unencrypted web)
  HTTPS   - TCP 443 (encrypted web)

File Transfer:
  FTP     - TCP 21 (control), 20 (data)
  SFTP    - TCP 22 (via SSH)
  SMB     - TCP 445 (Windows shares)

Directory/Name Services:
  DNS     - TCP/UDP 53
  LDAP    - TCP 389
  LDAPS   - TCP 636

Mail:
  SMTP    - TCP 25/587 (sending)
  IMAP    - TCP 143/993 (receiving)
  POP3    - TCP 110/995 (receiving)

Management:
  SNMP    - UDP 161/162
  NTP     - UDP 123
  DHCP    - UDP 67/68
```
teachingBlocks.explanation: Knowing port numbers lets you quickly identify traffic, write firewall rules, and troubleshoot connectivity. Well-known ports (0-1023) are assigned by IANA. The pattern of secure alternatives (22 vs 23, 443 vs 80, 993 vs 143) reflects the industry's move toward encryption. When troubleshooting, checking if the expected port is open is a quick diagnostic step.

surfaceVariants.description: Write firewall rules for a web server

data.requirement: Allow HTTP, HTTPS, SSH; deny all else

hints: SSH (22) is the secure alternative to Telnet (23)
DNS uses both TCP and UDP port 53

commonErrors.remediation: HTTP=80 (plain), HTTPS=443 (secure). The 'S' for secure is the higher number.
DNS, DHCP, SNMP, NTP use UDP for lightweight queries
